summary: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms. This chapter sets up the vocabulary — prokaryote vs eukaryote, the cell theory, and why size matters — used for every chapter after it.
key_points: Cell theory — all organisms are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; cells arise only from pre-existing cells.
Prokaryotic cells (bacteria, archaea) have no nucleus — DNA sits free in the cytoplasm.
Eukaryotic cells (plants, animals, fungi) have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Surface-area-to-volume ratio limits how large a single cell can grow before diffusion becomes too slow.
recap: Two cell types, one theory, one size limit — everything else in this unit builds on this page.

summary: Every organelle in the cell has one job and does it well. Think of the cell as a tiny factory — the nucleus is the office, mitochondria the power plant, ribosomes the assembly line.
key_points: Nucleus — houses DNA, controls gene expression, wrapped in a double membrane (nuclear envelope).
Mitochondria — site of aerobic respiration, produces ATP; has its own DNA (endosymbiotic origin).
Ribosomes — build proteins from mRNA; free-floating or attached to rough ER.
Golgi apparatus — modifies, sorts and packages proteins for secretion.
Cell membrane — phospholipid bilayer, selectively permeable, controls what enters/exits.

recap: Nucleus = control, mitochondria = power, ribosomes = build, Golgi = ship, membrane = gatekeeper.

summary: Genetics explains how traits pass from parent to offspring. Mendel's pea plants gave us the first rules — dominant and recessive alleles — long before anyone had seen a chromosome.
key_points: Allele — a version of a gene; organisms carry two per gene (one from each parent).
Dominant vs recessive — a dominant allele masks a recessive one in a heterozygote.
Genotype is the allele pairing (e.g. Aa); phenotype is the observable trait.
Punnett squares predict offspring ratios from a cross of two known genotypes.
recap: Genotype is the code, phenotype is what you see — Punnett squares just do the arithmetic between them.

summary: Move across or down the periodic table and properties shift in predictable directions — because you're really just changing how tightly the nucleus holds its electrons.
key_points: Atomic radius — decreases across a period (more nuclear pull), increases down a group (new shells).
Ionisation energy — increases across a period, decreases down a group.
Electronegativity — highest top-right of the table (excluding noble gases), lowest bottom-left.
Metallic character — increases down and to the left; nonmetals cluster top-right.

data.caption: fig. 2.1 — direction of increasing electronegativity & ionisation energy

recap: Across a period: smaller, harder to ionise, more electronegative. Down a group: the opposite.

summary: Three short statements that describe almost every everyday motion you'll ever see — from a dropped pencil to a rocket launch.
key_points: 1st law (inertia) — an object at rest stays at rest, in motion stays in motion, unless acted on by a net force.
2nd law — F = ma. Acceleration is directly proportional to net force, inversely proportional to mass.
3rd law — for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
recap: No force, no change (1st). Force causes acceleration (2nd). Forces come in pairs (3rd).
